Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette: Michael, a 37-year-old African American psychologist, has been struggling with debilitating symptoms since he was sexually assaulted in his office two years ago. The event occurred when he was alone on a late evening, and an intruder forced entry into the locked room where Michael was working on patient files. This traumatic experience left profound marks on Michael’s life. Initially, Michael found it difficult to return to his work as a psychologist, particularly due to the triggers that emerged from the incident. Being in a locked or confined space now sends waves of panic through him, and he finds himself hypervigilant whenever he is alone with men or hears comments about sexual violence. These triggers are potent because they remind Michael of the helpless and unsafe environment during his assault. Michael’s sense of threat is palpable; he feels constantly on edge, unable to relax even in seemingly safe environments. He has come to believe that he must always be alert and aware of his surroundings, positioning himself so that his back is against a wall where he can see everything happening around him. This constant state of vigilance makes it difficult for Michael to fall asleep at night because the need to remain alert persists even in his bedroom. Michael’s negative appraisals have deepened over time, contributing significantly to his heightened sense of threat and reactivity to triggers. He has come to believe that he will never fully recover from this trauma, leaving him feeling hopeless about his future. This belief exacerbates his feelings of vulnerability and helplessness, reinforcing the idea that he cannot prevent bad things from happening again. Consequently, Michael’s hypervigilance increases as these negative thoughts spiral into a self-reinforcing cycle. Michael also believes that others can see the trauma imprinted on him just by looking at him. This belief makes social interactions more challenging and contributes to his avoidance behaviors. For instance, he has started declining invitations to work-related events where he might encounter male colleagues alone in confined spaces, leading to professional isolation and strained relationships with peers. Over time, these negative appraisals have not only intensified Michael’s sense of threat but also increased the potency of his triggers. He avoids situations that remind him of the assault, such as being alone in locked rooms or around men, which has led to significant changes in how he conducts his daily work and social life. Despite recognizing the impact on his professional and personal life, Michael struggles to break free from this cycle. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident where he had a panic attack while meeting with a male colleague in his locked office. This event highlighted the urgency of addressing his symptoms before they further eroded his ability to function professionally. Michael is most afraid that his trauma will define his future and that he will never regain control over his life. He hopes for a way to alleviate these pervasive feelings of threat, hopelessness, and helplessness so that he can return to living a fulfilling life without constant fear.
